Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(m_d=\max A_d\).

First note that taking \(i=j\) gives
\[
|A_i|=i.
\]
Also, if \(a\mid b\), then
\[
|A_a\cap A_b|=\gcd(a,b)=a=|A_a|,
\]
so \(A_a\subseteq A_b\). In particular, for every divisor \(d\mid 250\), we have \(A_d\subseteq A_{250}\), and \(|A_{250}|=250\).

We will use the following observation. Suppose \(U\) is a union of some of the sets \(A_d\) with \(d\mid 250\), and let \(X\) be the maximum of the corresponding \(m_d\)'s. Then
\[
X\ge |U|.
\]
Indeed, all elements of \(U\) are at most \(X\). Since \(A_{250}\) contains \(250\) distinct positive integers, at least \(250-X\) elements of \(A_{250}\) are greater than \(X\) (if \(X<250\); otherwise the inequality is automatic). Those elements cannot lie in \(U\), so they must lie in \(A_{250}\setminus U\), which has size \(250-|U|\). Thus
\[
250-X\le 250-|U|,
\]
so \(X\ge |U|\).

Now compute three union sizes:
\[
|A_{125}\cup A_{50}|=|A_{125}|+|A_{50}|-|A_{125}\cap A_{50}|=125+50-25=150,
\]
so
\[
\max(m_{125},m_{50})\ge 150.
\]
Since \(m_d\ge d\), we have \(m_{125}\ge125\) and \(m_{50}\ge50\), hence
\[
m_{125}+m_{50}\ge 200.
\]

Similarly,
\[
|A_{25}\cup A_{10}|=25+10-5=30,
\]
so
\[
\max(m_{25},m_{10})\ge 30,
\]
and therefore
\[
m_{25}+m_{10}\ge 40.
\]

Also,
\[
|A_5\cup A_2|=5+2-1=6,
\]
so
\[
\max(m_5,m_2)\ge 6,
\]
and hence
\[
m_5+m_2\ge 8.
\]

Finally, \(m_{250}\ge250\) and \(m_1\ge1\). Therefore
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} m_d
= m_{250}+(m_{125}+m_{50})+(m_{25}+m_{10})+(m_5+m_2)+m_1
\ge 250+200+40+8+1=499.
\]

It remains to show that \(499\) is attainable.

For each positive integer \(d\), choose a set \(B_d\) with \(|B_d|=\varphi(d)\), with all the \(B_d\)’s pairwise disjoint. For the divisors of \(250\), choose
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For all other \(d\), choose \(B_d\) disjoint from these and using positive integers larger than \(250\).

Define
\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} B_d.
\]
Because the \(B_d\)’s are disjoint,
\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{d\mid i,\ d\mid j}B_d=A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]
Also,
\[
|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}|B_d|=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n.
\]
Thus \(|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)\).

Now the relevant maxima are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
d & \max A_d\\
\hline
1 & 1\\
2 & 2\\
5 & 6\\
10 & 10\\
25 & 30\\
50 & 50\\
125 & 150\\
250 & 250
\end{array}
\]
and their sum is
\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

Hence the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}
\]
